skyline.text: How a mis­er­able stu­dent nearly cost the world Oppenheimer
Ajay Shah traces one un­eth­i­cal cul­ture from Roy Cohn on­ward
The great physi­cist who mis­judged the scale of the Manhattan Project

brief.head: Art in the multiplex
brief.text: Christopher Nolan, Amit Varma said, brings the sen­si­bil­ity of the artis­tic film­maker to the big screen, and stu­dios trust him to try new things. {005-C01}

brief.head: America the backwater
brief.text: In the early 20th cen­tury, Ajay Shah said, America was a back­wa­ter. The Jewish ex­o­dus from Europe, and the move of its great in­tel­lec­tu­als, made it take off. {005-C02}

brief.head: A frail bridge
brief.text: Oppenheimer could both un­der­stand mod­ern physics and ex­plain it, Ajay Shah said, a rare and im­por­tant gift. “Human lan­guage is al­ways a frail bridge of metaphors.” {005-C03}

brief.head: Technician or thinker
brief.text: Ajay Shah sep­a­rates tech­ni­cians, who know one nar­row thing, from in­tel­lec­tu­als, who think about the world on a larger scale. Oppenheimer, he said, was not a nar­row tech­ni­cian. {005-C09}

brief.head: Memory runs short
brief.text: Descendants on both sides of the Oppenheimer af­fair still carry its mem­ory, Ajay Shah said. In India, peo­ple of in­flu­ence often lack it: “We’re very ahis­tor­i­cal today.” {005-C12}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: When a cul­ture fa­vors dull peo­ple, then that so­ci­ety ends up ex­press­ing those genes.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, arguing that culture, not raw talent, decides who rises to power

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah’s hero, and what his fall says about states
lead.head: Needed in war, hunted in peace

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 5

play.label: Hear the rise and the fall

body: Christopher Nolan’s *Oppenheimer* was still days from re­lease when Amit Varma and Ajay Shah recorded this episode. Shah ad­mit­ted to nerves: the film’s sub­ject had been part of his life since child­hood.
“Oppenheimer died when I was one year old, and that will come as a sur­prise to most peo­ple, but it is not an­cient his­tory,” Shah said. “I am a vis­i­tor from the 20th cen­tury.” {005-S01}
His fa­ther passed on many sto­ries. As a boy, Shah read Robert Jungk’s *Brighter Than a Thousand Suns* sev­eral times; as a PhD stu­dent, he found Richard Rhodes’s *The Making of the Atomic Bomb*.
## Right man, right time
Oppenheimer stud­ied at Göttingen, then the great cen­tre of sci­ence and math­e­mat­ics, in a golden age of physics.
When Leo Szilard saw how a bomb could work and Albert Einstein wrote to President Roosevelt, the Manhattan Project began, with Oppenheimer, 38, at its head.
“Oppenheimer was the right per­son at the right place at the right time,” Shah said: ex­per­i­men­tal­ist, the­o­rist and gifted en­gi­neer at once.

Shah in­sisted that the rest of the man was no sideshow. Oppenheimer learnt Sanskrit, backed the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War and moved in com­mu­nist cir­cles. That breadth and bo­hemian life, Shah ar­gued, was the source of his en­ergy. {005-C04}
## After the bomb
“And then, of course, no good deed goes un­pun­ished,” Shah said. Once the bomb had been ex­ploded, tra­di­tional power struc­tures began to as­sert them­selves.

Oppenheimer told Truman he felt he had blood on his hands over Hiroshima and Nagasaki, which, Shah be­lieves, made Truman very un­com­fort­able. {005-S06} Then he ques­tioned the need for a hy­dro­gen bomb.

He had an­gered bu­reau­crats by out-arguing them, and under McCarthyism he be­came the most fa­mous tar­get. A rigged process aired his pri­vate life; he was thrown out of pub­lic pol­icy and went off to Princeton.
The story has a coda. About two years ago, Shah said, after cit­i­zens dug through the ar­chives, the US gov­ern­ment ad­mit­ted its mis­take and re­stored his se­cu­rity clear­ance.
## Darts and dull peo­ple

Varma took a les­son from Oppenheimer’s mis­er­able stu­dent years, be­fore Göttingen, when he left a poi­soned apple on his physics tutor’s table. Education, Varma ar­gued, is one-size-fits-all, and ge­nius needs the right place.
“I think that the tragedy of Oppenheimer is not the Oppenheimer who was, but the many, many count­less Oppenheimers who never even were,” he said.

Shah widened the point: the world is or­gan­ised around dull peo­ple, and uses mav­er­icks only in spe­cial mo­ments. As Varma put it, “in ex­tra­or­di­nary times you have to look past the medi­ocrity of the sys­tem be­cause you need ex­tra­or­di­nary peo­ple.” {005-C06}
Then, Varma said, the medi­ocrity of the sys­tem takes over.
“We have seven bil­lion peo­ple in this world, and each of them is a dart,” Shah said. What shapes the world is the in­sti­tu­tions and the cul­ture that do the sort­ing. {005-C10}
The hosts closed with books. Shah’s was Rhodes’s his­tory of the bomb, which, he said, ev­ery­body should read. Varma’s was Robert Caro’s *The Power Broker*, a study, he said, of how power cor­rupts.
Varma’s talk on his own hero, after whom his on-screen co-host Freddy is named, moved to the next episode: the con­ver­sa­tion about Oppenheimer had been too de­light­ful to cut short.

second.label: Rule of law
second.head: The state owns up
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how citizens made the US government admit its mistake

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on a state admitting its mistake

body: In the last ten years, Ajay Shah said, a group of peo­ple dug into the ar­chives, using free­dom-of-information ac­cess in the United States, and showed how the legal process against J. Robert Oppenheimer had been rigged. {005-S07}

About two years ago, the gov­ern­ment owned up. It ad­mit­ted its mis­take and re­in­stated his se­cu­rity clear­ance. “Okay, the man is long gone, but this is very im­por­tant,” Shah said. “States are cruel, co­er­cive crea­tures and make mis­takes all the time.”

This, for Shah, is what makes a coun­try first-world: in­de­pen­dent peo­ple can chal­lenge the gov­ern­ment and get it to re­tract. Indians, he said, never ex­pect their state to admit a mis­take. {005-C11}

quote.text: Being a first-world coun­try means being a coun­try where in­de­pen­dent peo­ple are able to write let­ters and chal­lenge the United States gov­ern­ment.

third.head: Restraint can wait

pic.caption: Amit Varma on playing your shots

body: When Amit Varma joined Wisden in 2001, Tim de Lisle was his editor’s ed­i­tor; de Lisle later edited the *Wisden Almanac*.
His tips were mostly about clar­ity, and Varma still uses some of his ex­am­ples in the on­line writ­ing course he teaches. But one tenet stood out: when in doubt, play your shots.

Varma ad­mits he was a ter­ri­ble writer then, flam­boy­ant and al­ways show­ing off, and the re­sult was “rub­bish writ­ing”. Playing your shots, he said, also teaches you what not to do. “Restraint is some­thing you ar­rive at nat­u­rally and or­gan­i­cally over the years as you ma­ture as an artist.” {005-S09}
He ap­plies the rule to Christopher Nolan, whose *Interstellar* and *Tenet* move him less. He would “rather have some­one try­ing too hard than not try­ing at all”. {#tryhard}

p2.deck: From Göttingen to Princeton: the hero Ajay Shah grew up with, and the lessons the hosts drew

from1.head: Needed in war, hunted in peace

quote.text: He brings a sen­si­bil­ity of the artis­tic film­maker, the in­ti­mate drama, but he also cares about that cin­e­matic ex­pe­ri­ence.

box.title: The book on the bomb
box.text: Even read­ers who think they know lit­tle sci­ence should read Richard Rhodes’s *The Making of the Atomic Bomb*, Ajay Shah said, be­cause all great acts of cre­ation are human projects. He found it as a PhD stu­dent and calls it the best. {005-R01}

sections.label: Before the film
sections.head: An auteur, but at scale
sections.caption: Nolan, the auteur at scale
body: Amit Varma had not seen *Oppenheimer*: the episode was recorded on the Thursday be­fore its re­lease. But he is a big fan of Christopher Nolan, and it blows his mind that Nolan works within main­stream Hollywood.

For this film, Varma said, Nolan left Warner Brothers for Universal, be­cause Warner now re­leases its films on the big screen and HBO Max si­mul­ta­ne­ously. Nolan is a stick­ler for the big-screen ex­pe­ri­ence.

People tend to as­sume that in­ti­mate, artis­tic films go to OTT and spec­ta­cles to the the­atres. Nolan strad­dles both worlds, and has built enough cred­i­bil­ity to try new things rather than fol­low a tem­plate. “So I call him an au­teur at scale, as it were,” Varma said. {005-C01}
Denis Villeneuve, he said, does the same.
## Arrival, and a rest­less friend

Varma’s first Villeneuve film was *Arrival*, which he saw in Bangalore with their friend Madhu Menon. Fifteen min­utes in, Menon com­plained: “This is so slow. What is hap­pen­ing?” Varma was lov­ing it.

Villeneuve’s *Blade Runner 2049* was, to Varma, bet­ter than the orig­i­nal, which is say­ing a lot: Ridley Scott’s *Blade Runner* is a mas­ter­piece, and Scott was one of Nolan’s in­spi­ra­tions. {005-R12}

Ajay Shah was “trep­i­dated”. Oppenheimer’s story is hard to tell with­out car­i­ca­ture, he said, though he felt *Dunkirk*, which Varma called one of the great­est war films he had seen, told its story well. {005-J07}
~ Despite “a Marvel cin­e­matic uni­verse and other such garbage”, Varma in­sists this is a golden age of world cin­ema. {005-J06}

quote.text: He brings a sen­si­bil­ity of the artis­tic film­maker, the in­ti­mate drama, but he also cares about that cin­e­matic ex­pe­ri­ence.

art.caption: Amit Varma on Nolan, the auteur at scale

sections.label: The rise
sections.head: He lit up the room
sections.caption: the making of his hero
body: Ajay Shah told the life briskly. Oppenheimer grew up in America, did some ex­per­i­men­tal physics in Britain and then went to “that great tem­ple of the physics and the math­e­mat­ics of the early 20th cen­tury”, the University of Göttingen. He got his PhD there, Shah thought, in 1927. {#phd}
Back home, at Caltech and UC Berkeley, he was leg­endary for being sound on the deep ideas of mod­ern physics and for being able to ex­plain them.
At 38 he was made head of the Manhattan Project. Whenever he walked into a room, Shah said, he lit up the room, and the con­ver­sa­tion was al­ways bet­ter with him in it.
## Hip, not square
About a hun­dred years ago, he took the trou­ble to learn Sanskrit. Shah of­fered Indians an anal­ogy: “I’d chal­lenge peo­ple in India to go learn Aramaic. Okay? We don’t do that.” {005-J03}

He sup­ported the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War. His brother was in the Communist Party, and he had a lover deep in­side it. In the lan­guage of the 60s, Shah said, Oppenheimer was firmly hip. {005-S05}
~ General Groves, Amit Varma added, chose him be­cause he was good at ev­ery­thing ex­cept sports. “Kinda like you,” Varma told Shah. {005-J01}

quote.text: In the lan­guage of the 60s, the line be­tween hip and square, Oppenheimer was firmly hip.

sections.label: The fall
sections.head: Blood on his hands
sections.caption: McCarthyism’s most famous target
body: Once the bomb had been ex­ploded, Ajay Shah said, tra­di­tional power struc­tures began to as­sert them­selves. Oppenheimer told Truman he felt he had blood on his hands for Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and Shah be­lieves that made Truman very un­com­fort­able. {005-S06}

Edward Teller pushed for a hy­dro­gen bomb out of sci­en­tific cu­rios­ity. Oppenheimer asked what was gained by going from 20 kilo­tons of TNT, enough to de­stroy an en­tire city, to 200 and 2,000. {#kilotons}
He had the curse, Shah said, of know­ing more than any­body else in the room, and had of­fended the “gray, blood­less, pow­er­ful peo­ple” on the los­ing side.

McCarthyism made him its most fa­mous tar­get. Personal in­for­ma­tion, some of it dug out il­le­gally, was made pub­lic. Shah called it char­ac­ter as­sas­si­na­tion: “In today’s lan­guage, we would call it in­for­ma­tion war­fare.”
## Cohn’s long shadow
The chief coun­sel for Joe McCarthy who tried to sub­poena Oppenheimer, in 1954 “or was it 56”, Shah won­dered, was Roy Cohn, later Donald Trump’s men­tor. {005-S08}

Shah sees one na­tion­al­ist, power-hungry, un­eth­i­cal cul­ture run­ning from McCarthy and Cohn to Trump, with peo­ple like Oppenheimer on the other side. To say there are very fine peo­ple on both sides, he said, is “not a fair state­ment”. {005-J13}
~ Many of today’s ac­tors on both sides, Shah noted, are that generation’s chil­dren and grand­chil­dren.

quote.text: Now Roy Cohn is the evil ge­nius, the men­tor, the teacher, the philoso­pher, the guide of Donald J. Trump.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on McCarthyism’s most famous target

sections.label: The lesson
sections.head: The geniuses who never were
sections.caption: mavericks and mediocrity
body: Amit Varma took a dif­fer­ent les­son from Oppenheimer’s stu­dent years. Before Göttingen he was mis­er­able; had he not made that lucky move, Varma said, he might have been com­pletely wasted.

Buy potato chips and you get 40 flavours, be­cause mar­kets cater to dif­fer­ent needs. {#chips} Education, de­signed in the 19th cen­tury to churn out work­ers for the in­dus­trial rev­o­lu­tion, is one-size-fits-all.

Citing Karthik Muralidharan, he said India’s sys­tem is “op­ti­mized for sort­ing, not teach­ing”: it sorts out al­ready-bright minds for the IITs and IIMs, and passes for good ed­u­ca­tion. {005-C07}
## Mavericks on loan

Ajay Shah widened the point. Most power is con­trolled by peo­ple who are straight and nar­row, he said, and the mav­er­ick is held at a dis­tance. Only in spe­cial mo­ments can the world use such peo­ple.

His ex­am­ple was Ukraine, where crazy peo­ple built an Uber for ar­tillery be­cause the coun­try is fight­ing for sur­vival. {005-J14} Oppenheimer, like­wise, re­cruited the clever, not the obe­di­ent. When the war ended, the state no longer needed him.

Varma lamented academia’s ever-narrower silos, which end with some­one “spe­cial­iz­ing in some­thing like wheat pro­duc­tion in Ukraine be­tween the years 1836 to 1838”. {005-J02} Shah blamed jour­nal and fund­ing in­cen­tives.
~ Varma pointed to Jahnavi Phalkey’s *Atomic State*, about three sci­en­tists in 1940s India: once the ex­tra­or­di­nary times were over, nor­mal pol­i­tics took over.

quote.text: You’re forced into silos. And those silos get nar­rower and nar­rower as time goes by.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on mavericks and mediocrity

sections.label: Amit’s pick
sections.head: A broker and his city
sections.caption: a biography of a man and a city
body: Amit Varma’s pick was Robert Caro’s *The Power Broker*, a bi­og­ra­phy of Robert Moses, a bu­reau­crat who gath­ered so much power that even the gov­er­nor of New York was under his sway. {005-R03}
Varma reads it as three bi­ogra­phies: of a man, of New York City, and of how power cor­rupts.

Moses’s imag­i­na­tion of the city was top-down: he would build a fly­over or a bridge re­gard­less of the neigh­bour­hood. His great op­po­nent was Jane Jacobs, one of Varma’s in­tel­lec­tual he­roes, who ar­gued that cities are about peo­ple, not build­ings. {005-R05}
Varma half-remembered a Winston Churchill line; Shah sup­plied it: “We shape our build­ings and our build­ings shape us.” {005-J12}

In the 1920s and 30s, Varma said, Moses seemed a bril­liant, ide­al­is­tic vi­sion­ary. {005-C14} The book shows how power went to his ego and his pol­i­tics. “It is not just about power, it’s about all of us.”
## India’s mid­dle road

Ajay Shah said the Indian mid­dle class yearns for an au­thor­i­tar­ian gov­ern­ment to tell it where the park and the metro go. India needs an urban phi­los­o­phy that nei­ther ro­man­ti­cises in­for­mal­ity nor copies Chandigarh. {005-C15}
~ “I was born in Chandigarh,” Varma replied. They set­tled on Brasilia in­stead.

quote.text: An in­cred­i­ble study of how power cor­rupts, how power cor­rupts and cor­rodes the soul.

portraits.credit: C.M. Stieglitz, World Telegram staff photographer, public domain

quote.text: And that was the en­ergy, the cre­ativ­ity, the imag­i­na­tion, the in­tel­lec­tual charisma that man­aged to bring all that to­gether. You can­not sep­a­rate out these parts.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: An apple, a road, a factory and a very long book

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Oppenheimer’s miserable student years
stories.head: An apple for the teacher, poisoned
body: Before Göttingen, J. Robert Oppenheimer was, by all ac­counts, a bad stu­dent. So Amit Varma told it, as he turned from Ajay Shah’s hero to the hero’s early trou­bles.
His physics tutor be­rated him for not doing enough ex­per­i­men­tal work. Oppenheimer was think­ing about big ideas; he was ex­pected to get down and dirty in the lab.

A friend who came to his room, al­ways a chaotic mess, re­mem­bered what Oppenheimer told him: “I am hav­ing a pretty bad time. The lab work is a ter­ri­ble bore, and it is im­pos­si­ble to feel that I am learn­ing any­thing.” {#bore}
He was so un­happy that he left a poi­soned apple on his tutor’s table. For a long time, Varma said, peo­ple thought the story apoc­ryphal. But Oppenheimer ad­mit­ted to it.
The uni­ver­sity held an in­quiry. His par­ents were wealthy, and they made sure he was not ex­pelled, on the con­di­tion that he un­dergo some psy­chi­atric treat­ment.

Then he went to Göttingen, “a golden place where ev­ery­thing fit”, Varma said. He stud­ied under Max Born, who, Varma said, coined the term quan­tum physics, and had class­mates like Dirac and John von Neumann. Suddenly, he flour­ished.
Varma set his story be­side a su­per­mar­ket, where potato chips come in 40 flavours. If Oppenheimer had wanted chips or shav­ing cream, he would have got what­ever he wanted.
~ Had he not made that lucky move, Varma said, he might have been wasted. An ab­so­lute ge­nius was al­most lost, be­cause the world did not cater to his needs. {005-S02}
stories.why: Genius de­pends on find­ing the right en­vi­ron­ment, Varma ar­gued. An ed­u­ca­tion sys­tem built on one size for all, he said, wastes the many minds that do not fit its mould.
stories.postscript: At Göttingen, Varma added, Oppenheimer was ac­cused of being too ar­ro­gant and too con­fi­dent in him­self.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Oppenheimer’s poisoned apple

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the idea that made the bomb buildable
stories.head: The aha moment mid-road
body: Amit Varma quoted Ernest Rutherford say­ing that any­one who ex­pects a source of power from atoms “is talk­ing moon­shine”, and an early Albert Einstein say­ing nu­clear en­ergy would never be ob­tain­able. {005-J09} Ajay Shah’s reply: “You gotta look at the dates of those things.”
For a long time, Shah said, E = mc² looked like a cu­rios­ity. There was not the slight­est idea of the en­gi­neer­ing. Over the next 20 or 30 years, the pieces came to­gether.
Then Leo Szilard, cross­ing a road in London, had his aha mo­ment: neu­trons could trig­ger a chain re­ac­tion. For the first time, all the pieces clicked. {005-S03}
~ Fearing Hitler would get the bomb first, Szilard got through to Einstein, whose let­ter per­suaded President Roosevelt to start the Manhattan Project. {005-R23}
stories.why: Scepticism, Shah ar­gued, should be judged by when it was voiced. An idea can stay a cu­rios­ity for decades until one miss­ing piece makes it build­able, and then, sud­denly, it is an en­gi­neer­ing project.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Szilard’s road crossing

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the sheer scale of the Manhattan Project
stories.head: Turn America into a factory? Done
body: Niels Bohr had not been told about the Manhattan Project for a while, Ajay Shah said. When it was un­folded to him, he said it could not be done: “You’ll have to turn the en­tire United States into a fac­tory.” Later he con­ceded: “and you guys did.” {005-S04}
The world’s big­gest fac­tory ever built was built for ura­nium en­rich­ment, Shah said, and an even big­ger fa­cil­ity for pro­cess­ing plu­to­nium. These were chal­lenges on a ti­tanic scale.
A team of a cou­ple of thou­sand peo­ple, in­spired and led by Oppenheimer, took it through to the fin­ish line.
~ Elsewhere Shah put the or­gan­i­sa­tion Oppenheimer built at “3,000 or 6,000 in­ter­est­ing peo­ple”, re­cruited for being clever, not obe­di­ent. {#thousands}
stories.why: Even Niels Bohr mis­judged what in­spired lead­er­ship and or­gan­i­sa­tion could achieve. Shah warned against see­ing the re­sult as in­evitable: it took a par­tic­u­lar leader, at a par­tic­u­lar mo­ment, to bring all the pieces to­gether.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a biography that outgrew its binding
stories.head: A million words, minus Jacobs
body: In the 1960s, Amit Varma said, Robert Caro went to a pub­lisher with a bi­og­ra­phy of Robert Moses that he said would take a few months. It took him, Varma thinks, twelve or thir­teen years, and ran to al­most a mil­lion words.
The pub­lisher in­sisted on one vol­ume, be­cause of the lim­its of bind­ing, so it was cut to 800,000. Out went a book-length sec­tion that dealt mainly with Jane Jacobs.

Those 200,000 words, Varma said, are a book on Jacobs by one of the great­est bi­og­ra­phers who ever lived. {#jacobs} They have never been made avail­able; today an au­thor could put them on the in­ter­net.
~ Caro then turned to Lyndon Johnson, a project still going on, with one vol­ume left. {005-S10} His thor­ough­ness re­minded Varma of Borges’ map as big as the world. {005-R25}

quote.text: He ac­tu­ally took longer to write about Lyndon Johnson’s years in the Senate than Lyndon Johnson spent in the Senate.

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah asked whether Caro still had his early drafts. Varma was not sure.

quiz.q: What did Niels Bohr say the Manhattan Project would require, and what did he later concede?
quiz.a: Turning the en­tire United States into a fac­tory; later he said, “and you guys did.”

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, is the real tragedy not the Oppenheimer who was?
quiz.a: Because of the count­less Oppenheimers who never were, lost to one-size-fits-all ed­u­ca­tion.

quiz.q: Which lines from the Gita did Oppenheimer recall at the first bomb test, in Ajay Shah’s telling?
quiz.a: The Vishwarup lines: “I am be­come death, de­stroyer of the world.”

quiz.q: Who was Joe McCarthy’s chief counsel, and whom did he later mentor?
quiz.a: Roy Cohn, who be­came the men­tor and guide of Donald J. Trump.

quiz.q: What did Amit Varma say India’s education system is optimised for, citing Karthik Muralidharan?
quiz.a: Sorting, not teach­ing: it picks out the al­ready-bright and passes for good.

quiz.q: Which phrase of Jane Jacobs did Ajay Shah think about during the COVID lockdown?
quiz.a: “The bal­let of the streets”, dis­rupted by lock­down even though the build­ings re­mained.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 5. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Niels Bohr (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); J. Robert Oppenheimer (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Christopher Nolan (Republic of Korea, CC BY-SA 4.0); Denis Villeneuve (Raph_PH, CC BY 2.0); Harry S. Truman (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Roy Cohn (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Robert Moses (C.M. Stieglitz, World Telegram staff photographer, public domain); Jane Jacobs (Phil Stanziola, public domain); Robert Caro (Larry D. Moore, CC BY 4.0); Jorge Luis Borges (Grete Stern, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: The Making of the Atomic Bomb
shelf.creator: Richard Rhodes
shelf.why: It ex­plains the sci­ence while car­ry­ing a lay reader along.

shelf.title: Brighter Than a Thousand Suns
shelf.creator: Robert Jungk
shelf.why: It is the book that got Ajay deep into the Oppenheimer story and shaped how he thought about the world while grow­ing up.

shelf.title: The Power Broker
shelf.creator: Robert Caro
shelf.why: Caro’s mas­ter­piece works on three lev­els: a bi­og­ra­phy of Robert Moses, a bi­og­ra­phy of New York re­shaped by top-down plan­ning, and a study of how power cor­rupts an ide­al­is­tic man.

shelf.title: Robert Caro’s multi-volume biography of Lyndon Johnson
shelf.creator: Robert Caro
shelf.why: Amit ad­mires its ex­tra­or­di­nary rigor, jok­ing that Caro took longer to write about Johnson’s Senate years than Johnson spent in the Senate.

shelf.title: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
shelf.creator: Jane Jacobs
shelf.why: Jane Jacobs’s ar­gu­ment that cities are about peo­ple, not build­ings and high­ways, and grow or­gan­i­cally from the bot­tom up: spon­ta­neous order and metis against Robert Moses’s high mod­ernism.

shelf.title: How to Write Well
shelf.creator: Tim de Lisle
shelf.why: Amit calls it a lovely book on writ­ing that fo­cuses on clar­ity.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

shelf.title: Oppenheimer
shelf.creator: Christopher Nolan
shelf.why: Amit ad­mires Nolan for bring­ing artis­tic, in­ti­mate sen­si­bil­ity to big-screen spec­ta­cle.

shelf.title: Dunkirk
shelf.creator: Christopher Nolan
shelf.why: Amit, no Nolan fan­boy, calls it the best war film ever made; Ajay, who knows the pe­riod deeply, sees it as the model for let­ting real events carry the drama.

shelf.title: Arrival
shelf.creator: Denis Villeneuve
shelf.why: It brought a level of in­tegrity and thought Amit hadn’t ex­pected from a main­stream stu­dio film.

shelf.title: Blade Runner 2049
shelf.creator: Denis Villeneuve
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite films, which he loves even more than Ridley Scott’s orig­i­nal mas­ter­piece: a mag­nif­i­cent med­i­ta­tion on the shap­ing of the self and the na­ture of mem­ory.

shelf.title: Blade Runner
shelf.creator: Ridley Scott
shelf.why: Amit calls it a mas­ter­piece and notes that Ridley Scott was one of Nolan’s in­spi­ra­tions.

shelf.title: Our Unlucky Children
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that mar­kets give us forty flavours of potato chips and a thou­sand sham­poos while ed­u­ca­tion stays one-size-fits-all, built in the 19th cen­tury to pro­duce work­ers, be­cause mar­kets aren’t al­lowed to work there.

shelf.title: Fixing Indian Education (Episode 185 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
shelf.why: A deep dive with Karthik Muralidharan into what’s bro­ken in Indian ed­u­ca­tion and how to fix it, in­clud­ing his point that the sys­tem is op­ti­mised for sort­ing, not teach­ing.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: The Poetic Feminism of Paromita Vohra (Episode 339 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Paromita Vohra
shelf.why: Paromita Vohra makes the same point from a very dif­fer­ent field: or­gan­i­sa­tions ev­ery­where op­ti­mise for the mean and shut out peo­ple who think dif­fer­ently.

shelf.title: Jahnavi and the Cyclotron (Episode 319 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Jahnavi Phalkey
shelf.why: Jahnavi Phalkey on a 1940s tus­sle among three sci­en­tists over build­ing India’s physics in­sti­tu­tions, which shows nor­mal pol­i­tics re­turn­ing once ex­tra­or­di­nary times end.

shelf.title: Atomic State
shelf.creator: Jahnavi Phalkey
shelf.why: Jahnavi Phalkey’s his­tory of the early pi­o­neers of nu­clear sci­ence in India, in­clud­ing the 1940s strug­gle among three sci­en­tists in which one won out and the other two didn’t.

shelf.title: The Hedgehog and the Fox
shelf.creator: Isaiah Berlin
shelf.why: It frames Oppenheimer as some­one with fox-like range, from Sanskrit to phi­los­o­phy, who was also an ex­pert in sev­eral fields.

shelf.title: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Paul Graham’s two-axis map of thinkers (con­ven­tional or in­de­pen­dent, pas­sive or ag­gres­sive) that sin­gles out the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded as the loud­est voices and the real ob­sta­cle to new ideas.

shelf.title: Oppenheimer, Nullified and Vindicated
shelf.creator: Kai Bird
shelf.why: It tells how archival dig­ging led the US gov­ern­ment to admit it had wronged Oppenheimer.

shelf.title: The US Government order accepting its mistake on Oppenheimer
shelf.why: It is the pri­mary doc­u­ment of a state for­mally ad­mit­ting its error, which Ajay holds up as what a first-world state looks like.

shelf.title: Einstein’s Letter to President Roosevelt (1939)
shelf.creator: Albert Einstein
shelf.why: It is the let­ter that, after Szilard reached Einstein, per­suaded Roosevelt to start the bomb project be­fore Hitler could get there.

shelf.title: The enduring legacy of Leo Szilard
shelf.creator: Ashutosh Jogalekar
shelf.why: Background on the physi­cist whose chain-reaction in­sight while cross­ing a London road set the bomb project in mo­tion.

shelf.title: On Exactitude in Science
shelf.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
shelf.why: Borges’s one-paragraph para­ble of car­tog­ra­phers whose per­fectly ac­cu­rate map is as large as the em­pire and out of date the next mo­ment: no rep­re­sen­ta­tion can fully cap­ture re­al­ity.

shelf.title: Listen, The Internet Has SPACE
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It makes the point he states on air: the old page and bind­ing lim­its no longer apply, so today an au­thor could sim­ply put the rest on­line.

laughs.text: General Groves picked Oppenheimer be­cause he was good at ev­ery­thing, in­clud­ing met­al­lurgy, en­gi­neer­ing and chem­istry, ex­cept sports. Amit turns to Ajay: ‘Kinda like you, you know ev­ery­thing ex­cept sports, right? Bollywood per­haps.’

Amit’s car­i­ca­ture of aca­demic hyper-specialisation: some­one ‘spe­cial­iz­ing in some­thing like wheat pro­duc­tion in Ukraine be­tween the years 1836 to 1838’, which he ad­mits isn’t far from real spe­cial­i­sa­tions.
To show how rare Oppenheimer learn­ing Sanskrit was, Ajay of­fers an anal­ogy: ‘I’d chal­lenge peo­ple in India to go learn Aramaic. Okay? We don’t do that.’
Ajay names Chandigarh as the ex­treme of top-down plan­ning. Amit: ‘Well let me be clear about one thing. I was born in Chandigarh.’ They swap in Brasilia as the ex­am­ple in­stead.

Amit calls this a golden age of cin­ema de­spite ‘a Marvel cin­e­matic uni­verse and other such garbage’, then re­calls his friend Madhu Menon com­plain­ing 15 min­utes into Arrival: ‘This is so slow. What is hap­pen­ing?’

‘Trepidated’ be­comes the hosts’ made-up word for their feel­ings about Nolan’s film. Ajay ex­plains: ‘I’m scared of the movie being a mess. I’m scared of the movie hit­ting me too hard. I’m trep­i­dated.’
Bhagavad Gita: at the first bomb test, Oppenheimer re­called the Vishwarup lines, ‘I am be­come death, de­stroyer of the world’, from a text he had read after learn­ing Sanskrit.

Rutherford: ‘Anyone who ex­pects a source of power from these atoms is talk­ing moon­shine.’ Early Einstein: ‘there is not the slight­est in­di­ca­tion that nu­clear en­ergy will ever be ob­tain­able.’ Ajay’s re­join­der: ‘you gotta look at the dates of those things.’
Sitzfleisch, German for ‘sit­ting flesh’: Murray Gell-Mann’s ex­pla­na­tion of why Oppenheimer never won a Nobel Prize. Wolfgang Pauli sim­i­larly said he was good at ideas but not at cal­cu­la­tion.
Ajay on Oppenheimer’s bo­hemian streak: ‘in the lan­guage of the 60s, the line be­tween hip and square, Oppenheimer was firmly hip.’
Winston Churchill’s line, which Amit half-remembers and Ajay fin­ishes: ‘We shape our build­ings and our build­ings shape us.’

Right after trac­ing a line from McCarthy and Roy Cohn to Donald Trump, Ajay re­jects the idea that ‘there are very fine peo­ple on both sides’, say­ing his­tor­i­cal dis­tance shows that’s ‘not a fair state­ment.’
Ukraine’s ‘Uber for artillery’, which Ajay cites as mav­er­ick cre­ativ­ity that only wartime sur­vival al­lows in­side a mil­i­tary bu­reau­cracy.

Homi Bhabha and Vikram Sarabhai, whom Ajay names as India’s Oppenheimer-like fig­ures: re­mark­able peo­ple given rare op­por­tu­ni­ties, next to whom ‘a lot of mod­ern India seems dull in com­par­i­son.’
